title: Chapter 11 — Peculiar Effects Of The Love Of Physical Gratifications In Democratic Ages
paragraphs: One might suppose, from what has just been said, that the love of physical gratification must constantly drive the Americans into moral irregularities, disturb the peace of families, and threaten the security of society at large. That is not the case. The passion for physical gratification produces very different effects in democracies from those it produces in aristocratic nations. Sometimes an aristocracy — worn out by public affairs and glutted with wealth, amid the ruin of religious belief and the decline of the state — is gradually seduced into pursuing only sensual enjoyment. At other times the power of the monarch or the weakness of the people, without stripping the nobility of its fortune, forces it to stand apart from the administration of affairs. With the road to great undertakings closed, the aristocracy is left to the restlessness of its own desires. It then falls heavily back upon itself and seeks in bodily pleasures the forgetfulness of its former greatness. When the members of an aristocratic body are thus exclusively devoted to the pursuit of physical gratification, they usually concentrate in that direction all the energy they draw from their long experience of power. Such men are not content with the pursuit of comfort. They demand sumptuous depravity and splendid corruption. The worship they offer the senses is a gorgeous one, and they seem to compete in the art of degrading their own natures. The stronger, the more famous, and the freer an aristocracy has been, the more depraved it will then become. However brilliant its virtues may once have shone, I dare predict that they will always be outdone by the splendor of its vices.

The taste for physical gratification leads a democratic people into no such excesses. There, the love of well-being shows itself as a tenacious, exclusive, universal passion, but its range is limited. No one thinks of building vast palaces, of conquering or imitating nature, of ransacking the world to gratify one man's passions. Instead, people think of adding a few acres to their land, of planting an orchard, of enlarging a house, of always making life more comfortable and convenient, of avoiding trouble, and of satisfying the smallest needs without effort and almost without cost. These are small objects, but the soul clings to them. It dwells on them closely, day after day, until in the end they shut out the rest of the world, and sometimes even come between the soul and heaven.

It may be objected that this can only apply to members of the community in humble circumstances, and that wealthier people will display tastes like those they had in aristocratic ages. I dispute the claim. When it comes to physical gratification, the richest members of a democracy show tastes not very different from those of the people — whether because, having risen from the people, they actually share those tastes, or because they feel it is their duty to conform. In democratic society the public appetite has taken a moderate and quiet course to which everyone is bound to conform. It is as hard to depart from the common rule by one's vices as by one's virtues. Rich men living in democratic nations are therefore more intent on providing for their smallest wants than on extraordinary enjoyments. They gratify a host of petty desires without indulging in any great outbursts of passion. They are thus more likely to become enervated than debauched. The particular taste men of democratic ages have for physical enjoyments is not by nature opposed to the principles of public order. On the contrary, it often needs order in order to be satisfied. Nor is it hostile to regularity of morals, for good morals contribute to public tranquility and favor industry. It may even often be combined with a kind of religious morality. Men wish to be as well off as they can in this world without forgoing their chance of another. Some physical gratifications cannot be indulged in without committing a crime, and from these they strictly abstain. Others are sanctioned by religion and morality, and to these the heart, the imagination, and life itself are given up without reserve — until, in snatching at these lesser goods, men lose sight of those more precious possessions that constitute the glory and greatness of mankind. The reproach I direct at the principle of equality is not that it leads men astray in pursuit of forbidden enjoyments, but that it absorbs them entirely in the pursuit of allowed ones. By this means a kind of virtuous materialism may ultimately establish itself in the world — one that would not corrupt but enervate the soul, and silently slacken its springs of action.
